newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - New Russian cabinet forging ahead with reform.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New Russian cabinet forging ahead with reform.

text.p: Russia's rejuvenated cabinet is tackling intractable economic problems with renewed vigour, and for the first time in years the administration seems united in its intent to radically reform the economy, analysts say.
The new team, spearheaded by First Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, has taken on Soviet-era monopolies whose political clout made them seem untouchable.
For the first time in post-Soviet history, the cabinet appears to be united and political opposition to it is weak.
It enjoys full backing from President Boris Yeltsin, which has allowed the cabinet to undertake tasks which previous administrations have failed to tackle.
The only real danger is that the good long-term prospects could be destroyed by a looming financial crisis.

The explosive issue of housing subsidies has been tackled, and, with a little prodding from the International Monetary Fund, a new tax code has been drawn up to replace the current confusing and contradictory set of taxes.

But with the economy stubbornly refusing to spark, and a financial crisis threatening to make government unworkable, the question is whether the reforms can deliver their payoff before a political reaction sets in.

"The atmosphere is much more positive and you get a sense that things are moving. Now it's a case of having the political will to make it work," said Vlad Konovalov, chief economist of the World Bank in Moscow.
YELTSIN RELAUNCHED REFORMS
The present reform drive was announced by Yeltsin in his state of the nation address in March, which marked his return to active government after months of electioneering and sickness.

Yeltsin promised to get tough collecting taxes, which are coming in well below budgeted levels, preventing the government from paying wages and other bills, and promised a new tax code to replace the current confusing and unfair system.

He also called for natural monopolies, such as oil and electricity, rail and oil pipelines, to be made more efficient so that their prices could fall, and Nemtsov, brought into the cabinet soon after the speech, wasted no time in tackling the two biggest -- gas and electricity.

Russia's national gas company Gazprom is the world's biggest gas concern, accounting for about a quarter of world gas output. It was once headed by current prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, giving it huge political pull.
The secretive gas monopoly is one of Russia's richest companies. But because many of its customers are behind in paying their bills, it too owes billions of dollars.
Nemtsov, who is also Energy Minister, said last month Gazprom owed 14.8 trillion roubles ($2.6 billion) in federal taxes. The first aim of the cash-strapped government is to get Gazprom to pay up.

A commission headed by Nemtsov is to supervise Gazprom, and the government, dissatisfied with its poor dividend earnings, will review the arrangement under which most of its 40 percent stake is managed by Gazprom chief executive Rem Vyakhirev.
The government rules out breaking up Gazprom, but non-core activities will be hived off, key functions will be separated and other producers will be given access to its gas pipeline.

Nemtsov has also moved on another Soviet-era behemoth, the national electricity utility Unified Energy System (UES). UES, Russia's biggest company, owns and operates the national transmission grid, owns several power stations directly and has large or controlling stakes in 70 of Russia's 72 regional "energo" power companies.

Nemtsov has brought in a banker from his old base of Nizhny Novgorod, Boris Brevnov, to be the new head of UES, which has already become more shareholder-friendly, issuing Global Depositary Receipt (GDR) share lookalikes.

A true wholesale market for electricity will be set up, allowing the energos to sell across the country to industrial consumers who need power, bringing down prices, and giving independent producers access to the grid.

Another vital structural reform, and one which will touch the lives of millions, is a plan to end housing subsidies, put recently by Yeltsin at a staggering 119 trillion roubles a year. This will end low Soviet-era rents, and target aid more closely.

Nemtsov, who is one of Russia's most popular politicians, has been given responsibility for housing reform and also for tackling corruption in the civil service, whose cost in dragging down business activity is untold billions of dollars a year.

The government is tackling another potential source of corruption -- the system under which public money is disbursed through "authorised" commercial banks, enabling banks to divert and invest the funds before paying them out.
Chubais is setting up a Western-style treasury system to handle government payments, and Yeltsin has ordered authorised banks to be selected by open tender.
SIGNS REFORM DRIVE IS PAYING OFF
The energy of reformers contrasts strongly with 1996, when policy drifted as the government was caught up with the presidential election campaign and then Yeltsin's illness.
"Structural reform had stalled completely in 1996, and 1997 provides a real window of opportunity after an election year," said the World Bank's Konovalov.
There are already signs the reform drive is paying off.
Revenues, only 65 percent of budgeted levels in the first four months, picked up in March and April. Gazprom's demand for cash to pay its taxes has even caused the rouble to strengthen.

But the budget crisis has allowed the communist-dominated State Duma (lower house of parliament) to attack the government, as the revenue shortfall means the administration must present proposals for cuts in planned spending to the Duma.

The Duma shrank back from confrontation last Friday, asking for more details of government plans to raise extra revenue before considering the spending cuts. Ministers have said they will slash expenditure anyway as they have no other choice.
More worryingly, a promised revival of the economy this year has so far failed to materialise, and ministers have again put back their forecasts of growth.

Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of economic activity, was 0.1 percent higher than a year earlier in January, prompting officials to hail the start of recovery after seven years of contraction, but in the first four months of this year GDP was flat, year-on-year.

"I think we have to wait until 1998 before we see the pay-off," said Simon Johnson, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who edits Russian Economic Trends, published by the European Union expert advisory service and the Russian government Working Centre for Economic Reform.
"I don't think the recovery, when it comes, hopefully in 1998, will be a big Polish-style boom," he added.
The radicalism of the Chubais-Nemtsov team has already attracted criticism, and not just from the communist opposition.

A front-page commentary in the liberal daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta this month, entitled "The incredibly rising cost of the reformers' errors could lead to the most dismal consequences for the country's economy and population" denounced Nemtsov's plans as the experiment of an adventurer.

"The success of the reforms cannot be guaranteed mainly because they lack the most elementary prerequisites -- sufficiently high qualifications and experience in managing the economy in the young reformers," it said.
But for now the reformers are basking in the backing of a rejuvenated Yeltsin with his eye on the history books. They know that time is on their side.
"The team is pretty secure politically. It knows it's got a few years to produce results," said MIT's Johnson. ($ = 5754 Russian Roubles)
